The work, titled **“Entropa,”** was created by Czech sculptor **David Černý**, known for provocative public art. Unveiled in Brussels in 2009, the large-scale piece presented a map of the European Union in which each member state was depicted through a deliberately crude national stereotype.

At first, the project was described as a multinational collaboration, with each country allegedly represented by an artist from that nation. A brochure accompanying the installation listed fictional names and biographies. The **Netherlands** appeared partly submerged, with only minarets visible above the water, while **Denmark** was rendered in a way some linked to the controversy over cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad. The **United Kingdom**, long skeptical of deeper EU integration, was notably absent from the map.

Černý defended the installation as a work of satire aimed at exposing the clichés, prejudices and self-images that shape European politics. He said the hoax was intended as part of the concept, arguing that Europe itself is built on myths, misunderstandings and competing national narratives.

Czech officials, however, were caught off guard. The Czech government had promoted the installation as a symbol of European cooperation during its EU presidency, only to face embarrassment when the false authorship was revealed. Officials apologized for the deception, while also emphasizing that the country supported artistic freedom.

The sharpest reaction came from Bulgaria, whose government demanded that its section be removed or covered. The depiction was later concealed, but the broader installation remained on display.

The controversy turned **“Entropa”** into one of the most talked-about artworks associated with an EU presidency. Supporters praised it as a bold challenge to European complacency, while critics called it insulting, immature and diplomatically irresponsible.

For Černý, the uproar was in keeping with a career built on provocation. For the EU, the episode became an uncomfortable reminder that the union’s motto — “United in diversity” — can be tested not only by policy disputes, but also by jokes about how Europeans see one another.

Eventually, the Bulgarian section of the installation was **covered with black cloth**, a rare act of partial censorship inside an EU venue and a visible sign of how far the backlash had escalated.

Other countries also expressed discomfort, though not all issued formal protests. Some officials privately bristled at the caricatures, while others publicly tried to laugh them off. The incident nonetheless became an early embarrassment for the Czech EU presidency, which had hoped to project confidence and cultural sophistication.

## The hoax deepens the scandal

The diplomatic damage was compounded by the discovery that Černý had misled the Czech government.

The original presentation described “Entropa” as a joint work created by artists from every EU country — a symbolic European collaboration. Catalog materials included names, biographies and statements attributed to these supposed artists. Journalists and art observers soon began checking the claims and found inconsistencies. Some of the named artists could not be located; others appeared to be fictional.

Černý then admitted that the project had been produced by him and collaborators in the Czech Republic. He said the deception was part of the artwork’s concept, intended to expose stereotypes and assumptions about European identity.

That explanation did little to calm the political reaction. The Czech government had helped finance and promote the installation under the belief — or at least the public claim — that it was a multinational project. Officials suddenly found themselves defending not only controversial satire, but also a hoax carried out under government patronage.

## Prague apologizes, but defends artistic freedom

The Czech government moved quickly to limit the fallout. **Alexandr Vondra**, then deputy prime minister for European affairs and a leading official in charge of the Czech EU presidency, publicly apologized to Bulgaria and to anyone offended by the work. He acknowledged that the government had been misled about the authorship of the installation.

Prague emphasized that it had not intended to insult any EU member state and expressed regret over the false presentation of the project. Czech officials said they had expected a provocative but legitimate European collaboration, not a single-artist fabrication.

At the same time, the government stopped short of removing the entire piece. Officials sought to balance diplomatic damage control with a defense of artistic expression, arguing that satire inevitably provokes discomfort. The result was an uneasy compromise: the installation remained in place, while Bulgaria’s panel was covered.

Černý also apologized for deceiving the government and for offending Bulgaria, though he defended the work’s satirical purpose. Reports at the time said he offered to return public money connected to the commission, as the government examined how the project had been approved and presented.

## A presidency overshadowed by satire

For the Czech Republic, the timing could hardly have been worse. The country had only just taken over the rotating presidency of the EU Council, a role meant to demonstrate administrative competence and diplomatic maturity. Instead, one of its most visible cultural gestures became a symbol of misjudgment.

The scandal also reflected broader tensions within the EU: between older and newer member states, between national pride and supranational identity, and between free expression and diplomatic etiquette. “Entropa” suggested that Europe’s unity was assembled from clichés, resentments and fragile symbols — and the reaction to the piece arguably proved its point.

Yet the controversy left a lingering question: was the artwork a brilliant provocation that exposed Europe’s inability to laugh at itself, or an officially sponsored prank that humiliated partners and embarrassed its patrons?

For Černý, already known for irreverent and politically charged public art, the uproar reinforced his reputation as one of Europe’s most provocative artists. For the Czech government, it became a cautionary tale about the risks of turning satire into state diplomacy.

In the end, “Entropa” succeeded in commanding attention — but not in the way Czech officials had hoped. What began as a model kit of Europe became a real-time demonstration of how easily the pieces of European unity can come apart.
